title: ForgeTwin
pitch: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am both a mechanical engineer and a web developer , and this project came from combining these two parts of my experience. In mechanical engineering, having a good idea is only the beginning. The idea must become real geometry, materials, joints, forces, sensors, controls, and measurable results. In web development, I learned how a good interface and AI can make a complicated tool easier for more people to use. This made me ask one question: What if AI could do more than generate a picture or description of a machine? What if it could enter the same engineering workspace as the human, build the machine part by part, test it, see what failed, and improve it? This is why I built ForgeTwin. I wanted someone to describe a physical goal in normal language, without knowing every CAD command, and then watch an AI agent turn that goal into an editable, animated, and testable mechanical system. As an engineer, one principle was very important to me: A design should not be trusted only because it looks convincing. It should be tested with physics and evidence. Don’t generate it. Engineer it. What it does ForgeTwin is a browser-based AI engineering sandbox. The user describes a machine or mechanical goal, and ForgeTwin creates a versioned physical world from reusable parts. For example, a user can ask: “Build a conveyor that sorts red and blue boxes at 20 boxes per minute.” “Build an electric go-kart with four wheels, steering, accelerator and brake pedals.” “Build a brazing fixture that positions a heat exchanger and two copper pipes within 2 mm.” ForgeTwin then: Understands the requested machine, functions, and measurable requirements. Creates an engineering plan instead of returning only text. Breaks the design into assemblies and reusable low-level components. Gives every component dimensions, material, mass, position, and orientation. Adds physical connections, joints, motors, sensors, actuators, and control logic. Builds the machine in an interactive 3D workspace while the user watches. Runs a fixed-step 60 Hz Rapier simulation. Reads telemetry, collisions, movement, and requirement measurements. Finds the reason when a requirement fails. Changes the related geometry, physical property, actuator, motor, or controller and runs the test again. The app is not limited to conveyors. Its 39-part reusable vocabulary covers structures, power transmission, controls, road vehicles, motorcycles, aircraft, rotorcraft, tracked mobility, and articulated robots. It can compose cranes, lifts, bicycles, go-karts, motorcycles, cars, rovers, robotic arms, humanoid robots, gearboxes, suspension systems, airplanes, helicopters, solar trackers, bridges, warehouse systems, agriculture machines, recycling systems, HVAC fixtures, medical lifting mechanisms, and new systems made from smaller primitives. The current app includes 19 editable challenge briefs , but these are examples, not locked machine templates. The user can change the prompt, dimensions, load, speed, or target. If a special component is not already available, the planner can build it from lower-level parts such as beams, plates, tubes, shafts, wheels, pulleys, joints, sensors, and motors. The user can also: Use the built-in AI without entering credentials, or temporarily use their own OpenAI API key. Edit the existing design with natural-language chat instead of starting over. Select, move, resize, and rotate parts in X, Y, and Z. Orbit the full camera through 360 degrees with mouse or touch. Use a rotation gizmo, snapping, or numeric angle entry. Lock a manual change so the AI redesigns around it instead of moving it back. Animate the operating sequence of different machine families. Run physics and replay a failure in slow motion. Use X-Ray Mode to inspect joints, sensor paths, axes, collision boxes, actuator paths, and velocity information. Inspect requirement evidence and see what passed, failed, or was not evaluated. Undo changes, restore revisions, and compare a failed design with the improved design. Export the current world as PNG, JPG, PDF, STL exchange geometry, or complete ForgeTwin JSON data. How I built it ForgeTwin is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, and Zod . The main idea is that the machine is not saved as one opaque 3D model. It is stored as a shared engineering graph containing: Assemblies and individual bodies Dimensions, materials, mass, and rigid-body properties Position, rotation, and machine orientation Mechanical, power, and signal connections Fixed, revolute, prismatic, spherical, spring, rope, gear, and belt joints Motors, sensors, actuators, and control rules Simulation runs, telemetry, collisions, and failure evidence Human-owned edits and immutable revision history The 3D editor renders this graph procedurally. The same graph is used by the human interface, the built-in model agent, the physics simulator, the activity feed, exports, and an external WebMCP agent. The hosted AI uses GPT-5.6 Sol through the OpenAI Responses API . To keep generation faster and more reliable, the model creates a compact engineering intent: the object identity, architecture, motion, controls, primitive vocabulary, and requirements. ForgeTwin then expands that intent into the complete body-and-joint graph, validates it, repairs safe topology problems, and executes the design through guarded tools. The hosted key stays on the server, so judges can use the full AI experience without adding a key. A visitor can still connect their own key for the current browser tab. That key is kept only in memory and is not stored. If model access is unavailable, ForgeTwin also has a deterministic local engineering path for the main design, physics, optimization, and supported chat-edit operations. I also created one universal coordinate convention for every machine: +X is front, -X is rear, +Y is up, -Z is left, and +Z is right . This helped fix many problems with lights, wheels, propellers, steering, windshields, and joint axes. The design validator checks for missing supports, hubs, axles, joints, steering links, bad proportions, wrong orientations, floating components, incorrect joint axes, overlaps, blocked windshields, and unrequested systems. For example, a go-kart uses front wheel hubs, spindles, steering knuckles, separate kingpin axes, tie rods, a steering rack, column, and Ackermann-style steering instead of making the whole wheel rotate around one incorrect axis. Rapier runs the connected rigid-body world at a fixed 60 Hz and records replay frames and collision events. Some advanced engineering results, including aerodynamics, flexible cables, structural stress, detailed tire behavior, and some manufacturing processes, still use clearly labeled reduced-order checks. ForgeTwin is a concept-validation sandbox, not a replacement for certified CAD, FEA, CFD, medical approval, or safety analysis. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is what makes ForgeTwin an AI-operable engineering workspace instead of only a website with an AI button. ForgeTwin exposes 29 small, typed, state-aware WebMCP tools , including: inspect_workspace inspect_primitive_catalog set_design_goal create_assembly create_component set_dimensions , set_material , and set_mass move_component and rotate_component connect_components and create_joint add_motor , add_sensor , and add_actuator set_motor_speed , set_sensor_range , and set_actuator_timing set_control_logic and update_control_logic run_simulation inspect_telemetry , inspect_failure , and measure_constraint optimize_design remove_component and remove_joint compare_designs and restore_revision I did not create one giant generate_machine tool. The agent must inspect the current world, create parts, connect them, run the simulation, read the evidence, and make bounded changes. Every tool call is visible in the activity feed. This matters for human and AI collaboration. If I move a camera, sensor, or other component by hand, ForgeTwin creates a new revision and marks the transform as human-owned. The agent reads this new shared state and can redesign the rest of the machine without silently removing my decision. The built-in chat uses the same idea. It receives the current graph, selected component, latest measurements, human locks, and recent conversation. A request such as “move the right clamp 0.04 meters outward, preserve my camera position, and rerun the test” becomes a guarded change to the existing world, followed by a new simulation and revision. Without WebMCP, AI can give advice about the machine. With WebMCP, AI can work inside the engineering environment together with the human.
